title: What shall we do? (Luke 3:1–14)
hook: John tells the crowds: share your coat, don't cheat, don't extort

segments.voice: Yesterday, a twelve-year-old in the temple, about my Father's business, and then home to grow. Your line was growing is holy. Did you take your one small step? Day five hundred thirteen.

Luke opens this chapter like a news anchor reading the date. The fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius. Pontius Pilate governing Judea. Herod ruling Galilee. His brother Philip, another ruler named Lysanias, the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. Seven powerful names, one after another, the people with palaces and armies and seals. And then the sentence lands somewhere else entirely: "the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness." Not to the emperor. Not to the palace. To the son of an old priest, out in the empty country by the Jordan. And the crowds start walking out to hear him.
screen: `THE WORD CAME TO JOHN, IN THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: John doesn't flatter them. He greets them: "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" He tells them not to lean on their family tree, and he says the axe is already at the root of the trees. Then he says: "Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance." Repentance: a turn in how you live. And the crowd asks the obvious, honest question: "What shall we do then?" Here's what's surprising. John doesn't tell them to move to the wilderness, or to give up their trades. His answers are almost ordinary. To everyone: "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise." The coat here is the everyday tunic. If you have a spare, someone else is cold. Then tax collectors come to be baptized, and ask: "Master, what shall we do?" He doesn't tell them to quit. He says: "Exact no more than that which is appointed you." Collect what's owed. Don't pad the bill. Then soldiers come, men with weapons and power over civilians: "And what shall we do?" "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages." Three groups, three questions, three answers, and each one fits the person's actual job. In Luke, turning around doesn't start in a temple or a monastery. It starts at the closet, the tax booth and the checkpoint. It starts at your own counter, with your own receipts.
screen: then, large: `WHAT SHALL WE DO THEN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do the fair thing in one transaction. Settle, and breathe. Ask John's question about your own work and your own spending: what shall I do? Let your mind walk through a normal week. Where does money or time change hands? A bill you send. A tip you leave. Hours you log. A review you write. A price you set. A favor someone did that you never paid back. Somewhere in there is a small place where you could be a little more honest or a little more generous than you need to be. Let it come up. Don't make it dramatic. John didn't. If you pray, you can ask the crowd's question and listen. If you don't, simply name the one transaction. The bell holds the time.
Chiton, the Greek word for tunic, the garment worn next to the skin: the coat John tells the crowd to share, alongside his plain answers for tax collectors and soldiers too.
Your line: share your coat. Today, give away one thing you have two of, or make one transaction a little fairer than it has to be. Day five hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: In the Revised Common Lectionary, John's preaching from Luke 3 is read in Advent, and some Christian charities point to Luke 3:11 for coat drives and clothing closets.

fork.setup: you're a soldier standing in the crowd at the Jordan. you ask John what you should do. what does he say?
options: lay down your weapons and leave the army.
no violence, no false accusations, be content with your wages.
come and live in the wilderness with me.
fork.reveal: John answers each group in its own job: don't bully, don't lie about people, don't squeeze extra out of them.

original.note: Greek: a tunic, the garment worn next to the skin. the "coat" in Luke 3:11.

trapdoor: what you thought: John the Baptist, wild and fiery, shouting at everyone.
what it means: when people ask what turning around looks like, he gives each of them small, fair, concrete answers that fit their daily work.
what a scholar hears: the "coat" is a chiton, the inner tunic. John asks the person with a spare undergarment to give it to someone who has none.

notes: 'Seven powerful names' counts Tiberius, Pilate, Herod, Philip, Lysanias, Annas and Caiaphas (Luke 3:1–2). Confirm count.
The soldiers in 3:14 may have served Herod Antipas rather than Rome; the script does not say whose army.
Chiton as the inner tunic: standard lexicon gloss. Confirm.
Coat drives linked to Luke 3:11 in howItsDone is a general description; soften if needed.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: John's camel hair is in Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6, not Luke, so it is cut from this Luke day. Also cut the metanoia etymology (teach and match; match now uses the axe, 3:9), 'the people everybody resents' (an unsourced sweeping claim), and the lexical gloss of the coat as the garment next to the skin from the spoken text (kept in the original/trapdoor games for a Keeper to confirm); howItsDone softened.
